name: Guardian cryptic crossword, Penguin book 7 No 40

book.title: The New Penguin Book of The Guardian Crosswords, volume 7

entries.clue: The way immature Mary gets a guide to public opinion (5,4)

blocks.note: a street is a way, and St is its everyday short form
a raw recruit is an immature one, green and unseasoned
Poll is the old pet form of Mary, the same shortening that gives Polly

annotation.surface: The manner in which a green young Mary comes by a sense of what everybody thinks.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mary' looks like scene-setting and is a name cut down to four letters, the one a parrot is usually given. Nothing in the surface admits that the way at the front is a street.
annotation.definitionFit: A straw poll is an unofficial sounding of a handful of people, taken like a straw held up to see which way the wind of opinion blows.

entries.clue: Train or bus? (5)

blocks.note: the verb: to train a team is to put it through its paces
the long-distance vehicle, hired for the day trip rather than running a town route

annotation.surface: Choosing between two ways of getting there.
annotation.walkthrough: Both words look like vehicles, and the deception is entirely in the first: it is the verb for drilling a team. In Britain the vehicle sense is the long-distance one, distinct from the bus that stops on every corner.
annotation.definitionFit: To coach somebody is to train them, and a coach is also the vehicle itself — the same five letters for the instructor and the transport.

entries.clue: Bales out after crashing car, tight-lipped — that’s the least one can do (8,7)

indicatorNotes.after crashing: What comes out of a crash is not in the shape it went in, so the letters just named are to be rebuilt in some other order.

blocks.note: eight letters for the pile
the Mini is the small British car of the 1960s, named often enough to stand for any car
to keep mum is to say nothing

annotation.surface: A pilot ejects from a car he has just written off and will not say a word about it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bales out' is the aviator's escape on the surface and eight letters of fodder underneath, which is why the crash following it is an instruction rather than an event. The car and the silence are two separate pieces, not one phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: An absolute minimum is the smallest amount that will serve at all, which is what somebody doing the least they can get away with supplies.

entries.clue: Young children seen in rags (4)

blocks.note: the everyday word for them, borrowed from the young of a goat
the verb: to rag somebody is to tease them, and so is to kid them

annotation.surface: Small children going about in tattered clothes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rags' pretends to be the tattered clothing and is a verb, the one meaning to tease. Both senses of the answer began as slang: the young of a goat gave us the children, and ragging was schoolboy horseplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Kids are young children, the word taken from a goat's young; and to kid somebody is to rag them, pulling their leg for sport.

entries.clue: Passage for transport (8)

blocks.note: the way in — the door, hall or gateway by which you get inside
the verb, stressed on the second syllable: to carry somebody away with delight

annotation.surface: A corridor built for getting people about.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves read as traffic, and the second is the other word entirely: en-trance, to put into a trance, which is what carrying somebody away with delight amounts to. The stress shifts off the first syllable and the grid cannot show it.
annotation.definitionFit: An entrance is the passage or opening by which one goes in; and to entrance somebody is to transport them with delight.

entries.clue: One giving evidence in trial, if that is required initially (9)

blocks.note: a trial run of anything is a test of it
the clue's own word, taken exactly as it stands
i.e. is the Latin id est, which translates as 'that is'
the letter standing first in the word required

annotation.surface: A witness put in the box at the start of a trial, should one be needed at all.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trial' belongs to the definition's own world of courts and witnesses, and it is the first piece of wordplay, meaning a test. The three little words after it are taken at face value, spelling and all.
annotation.definitionFit: To testify is to give evidence on oath, so the agent noun names the person doing it in the witness box.

entries.clue: Heart doctor’s died after retiring (5)

indicatorNotes.after retiring: To retire is to go back the way you came, so the letters just assembled are read from the last of them to the first.

blocks.note: MO is the Medical Officer, the services' doctor, and the apostrophe-s comes along as a letter
ob. is the Latin obiit, 'died', the word cut on memorial tablets

annotation.surface: A doctor's death, reported after he had given up his practice.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Retiring' reads as leaving the profession and is the instruction to read backwards. The apostrophe supplies a letter rather than marking possession, which is allowed: punctuation never binds a solver.
annotation.definitionFit: The bosom is the breast, long used for the seat of the feelings — a bosom friend, a secret kept in the bosom.

entries.clue: Striking with fear in flight (5)

blocks.note: the participle of awe: filling somebody with dread and wonder
up off the ground and on the wing, as a bird is; the old adverb built with the prefix a-

annotation.surface: Something in the air that puts the fear of God into whoever looks up at it.
annotation.walkthrough: The two halves run into a single sentence, so there is no seam to find: fear and flight belong to the same picture. The second reading uses the old prefix a-, the one in asleep, ablaze and astride.
annotation.definitionFit: To awe is to strike with fear, which covers the participle; and awing is also on the wing, where anything in flight is.

entries.clue: Pulled ahead of one in public range (9)

indicatorNotes.in: In puts one thing inside another, so the letter named before it goes between the two pieces that follow instead of in front of them.

blocks.note: an overt act is one done in the open, publicly
a is the indefinite article doing duty for one
ken is the range of a person's sight or knowledge — beyond my ken

annotation.surface: Passing somebody where the whole public could see it happen.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Range' is neither the shooting sort nor the cooker: ken is how far a person's sight or understanding reaches. 'Public range' looks like one phrase and is two pieces with a letter driven between them.
annotation.definitionFit: To overtake is to pass somebody and get in front, so the participle is what the leader has done to everyone behind.

entries.clue: Consumes flounder in the vessel (8)

indicatorNotes.in: A thing put in another sits inside it, so the word named first goes between the letters of the one named after.

blocks.note: SS is the prefix on a steamship's name, as in SS Great Britain, and the two letters part to take the rest
to flounder about in mud is to wallow in it

annotation.surface: Somebody eating a flatfish on board ship.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flounder' is the fish on the surface and the verb underneath, and that one swap is the whole clue. SS before a ship's name is short for steamship.
annotation.definitionFit: To swallow food is to consume it, taking it down the throat.

entries.clue: ‘Army-stopper’ inventor exploded, making a big noise (4,9,6)

indicatorNotes.exploded: An explosion scatters whatever it goes off in, so the letters named before it come down in a different order.

blocks.note: nineteen letters for the pile; the quotation marks and the hyphen are punctuation for the surface only

annotation.surface: The man who devised a weapon for halting an army has blown himself up, loudly.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is built to fit the answer: somebody who explodes really is making a big noise. Every letter of the quoted nickname and of the word after it goes into the pile, which is why so long an entry has so short a clue.
annotation.definitionFit: A big noise is the idiom for a person of consequence, the one whose word carries — which is what the full form behind VIP spells out.

entries.clue: See 21
Bright day at US state (5)

blocks.note: Sun is the diary's short form for Sunday
NY is how an envelope abbreviates New York

annotation.surface: A fine day spent somewhere in America.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Day' is a named day of the week cut to three letters rather than daylight, though daylight is where the answer ends up. The state arrives abbreviated the way an address would have it.
annotation.definitionFit: Sunny weather is bright weather, sun rather than cloud overhead.

entries.clue: Once backward group one department sends forth (9)

indicatorNotes.backward: Backward means facing the other way, so everything named after it is read from its last letter to its first, all as one run.

blocks.note: ex- is the prefix for a former anything: an ex-minister was one once
a set is a group of people or things taken together
the Roman numeral for one
dep. is the short form of department on a form or a sign

annotation.surface: A formerly backward group and a single department now getting things out of the door.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backward' governs the three pieces after it at once rather than only the word beside it, so all nine letters of the tail turn together. 'Once' is the prefix ex-, the one in ex-wife.
annotation.definitionFit: To expedite something is to speed it on its way, sending it forth instead of letting it sit in a tray.

entries.clue: Carefully follow society chatter (5)

blocks.note: S is the standard short form for society, as in the initials of a learned one
chatter is talk, the idle kind

annotation.surface: Gossip going round the smart set.
annotation.walkthrough: Society chatter is one phrase on the surface and two separate pieces beneath it. The definition wants the hunter's word: to stalk a deer is to follow it with great care.
annotation.definitionFit: To stalk game is to follow it stealthily and with care, closing in without being noticed.

entries.clue: Attractive plants mistakenly regarded as reeds (7)

indicatorNotes.mistakenly regarded: Something regarded mistakenly has been taken for what it is not, and letters taken the wrong way are letters to be read in some other order.

blocks.note: seven letters for the pile, the little joining word included

annotation.surface: Handsome garden plants that somebody has wrongly taken for reeds.
annotation.walkthrough: The word joining the plants to what they were mistaken for is fodder rather than grammar, which is what makes the count come out. Reseda is the mignonette, grown in borders for its scent.
annotation.definitionFit: Resedas are mignonettes, garden plants raised for their sweet smell, so the definition names them by the class they belong to.

entries.clue: Youthful excesses in the tall grass? (4,4)

annotation.definitionNote: The second half describes the answer rather than naming it — a stand of wild oats is tall grass — and the question mark is the setter's admission of the stretch.

blocks.note: sowing them is what a young man is forgiven for doing before he settles down
Avena fatua, the wild oat, a coarse grass that comes up uninvited among the crop

annotation.surface: Young people misbehaving out in the long grass.
annotation.walkthrough: Sowing one's wild oats is the phrase the first half leans on, and the weed behind the phrase is a real one, tall enough to hide in. Both halves are the same two words, one figurative and one botanical.
annotation.definitionFit: To sow one's wild oats is to work youthful excess out of the system; and the wild oat itself is a tall coarse grass of field margins.

entries.clue: See 3
I run all over the place with a smile for celebrities (10)

indicatorNotes.all over the place: Things all over the place are not where they belong, so the letters named are to be gathered up in some other order.

blocks.note: four letters for the pile
six more letters, the article included

annotation.surface: Somebody dashing about cheerfully in pursuit of famous people.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I' is fodder rather than the setter talking, which is what keeps a ten-letter anagram hidden this long. A luminary is literally a giver of light, from the Latin for lamp.
annotation.definitionFit: A luminary is a shining light in some field, a name that draws a room's attention, which is what a celebrity is.

entries.clue: Give with others, but not fully — sorry about that (10)

indicatorNotes.not fully: What is not given fully stops short of its end, so the word beside it arrives one letter shorter than it was.
indicatorNotes.about that: To be about a thing is to be all round it, and 'that' points back at the piece just named, so the sorry word opens and closes on either side of it.

blocks.note: contrite is thoroughly sorry, penitent for what one has done
the clue's own three-letter word, docked of its last letter

annotation.surface: Someone chipping in alongside everybody else and apologising while they do it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'But' looks like the sentence's hinge and is the word being cut short. The definition is the whole opening phrase, because giving on your own is not it: contributing is giving into a pot other people are also filling.
annotation.definitionFit: To contribute is to put your share into a common fund that others are giving to as well, which is the 'with others' the definition insists on.

entries.clue: Promotions about fruit (not eastern) and nuts (7)

indicatorNotes.about: Something written about a subject goes all round it, so the first word opens up and what follows goes inside.
indicatorNotes.not: 'Not' takes away whatever it names, so the letter after it is struck out of the word it sits in.

blocks.note: promotions in a paper or a commercial break are ads, and the three letters split after the first
the fruit wanted is the lemon, and it goes inside with a letter missing
E is the compass point, eastern

annotation.surface: Advertisements for citrus that has not come from the East, and for nuts.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fruit' is left deliberately vague, and the one wanted is the lemon, handed over minus the E the bracket takes off it. 'Nuts' at the end is the definition rather than more of the shopping.
annotation.definitionFit: Almonds are the kernels sold and eaten as nuts, whatever a botanist would call the tree's fruit.

entries.clue: Smith, a ranting actor, one with a dual role? (6-3)

blocks.note: a ham is the actor who overdoes every line
a merman is man above and fish below, two natures in the one body

annotation.surface: A Mr Smith who overacts and appears to be playing two parts at once.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Smith' stands where a surname would beside an actor's name and is the trade instead, the man at the anvil. The dual role is not casting but a merman, half man and half fish.
annotation.definitionFit: A hammerman is the smith who swings the hammer at the forge, so the trade name and the old occupational surname point at the same worker.

entries.clue: Celebrate posh informal rally in an odd manner (10)

indicatorNotes.informal: Informal splits as in-formal, out of proper form, and letters out of form are letters not to be taken as they stand.

blocks.note: to sing of a victory is to celebrate it in song
U is upper class, from the U and non-U talk of 1950s Britain
five letters for the pile

annotation.surface: An upper-class gathering being celebrated in a peculiar way.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Informal' sits next to 'posh' as its opposite and is the anagram signal. U for upper class comes from Nancy Mitford's U and non-U, the vocabulary that was said to mark the classes apart.
annotation.definitionFit: Singularly means in a way that stands out as odd, the adverb of singular in its 'peculiar' sense rather than its 'one' sense.

entries.clue: Member of school is ashen, having caught low hit awkwardly (5-5)

indicatorNotes.having caught: Something caught is held inside whatever caught it, so the letters named next sit within the word in front of them.
indicatorNotes.awkwardly: Letters handled awkwardly come out in the wrong order, not the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: an ashen face is a pale one, and the four letters open after the first
six letters for the pile

annotation.surface: A pale-faced schoolboy who has taken a clumsy blow below the belt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'School' is the shoal, not the classroom — whales and porpoises travel in schools. The outer word breaks after a single letter, which is the step that hides the container.
annotation.definitionFit: Pilot whales move in large schools, the word used of whales as readily as of fish, so one of them is a member of a school.

entries.clue: Broadcasts features involving northern sergeant-major (9)

indicatorNotes.involving: To involve something is to wrap it in, so the word named first closes round the letters that follow.

blocks.note: a person's features of character are their traits, and the word opens after three letters
N is the compass point, northern
SM is the army's short form for sergeant-major

annotation.surface: A newspaper's features desk dealing with a sergeant-major from the north.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Features' is the newspaper section on the surface and means characteristics, the traits of a face. Two pieces go into the gap one after the other, which is rarer than a single insertion.
annotation.definitionFit: To transmit a programme is to send it out over the air, which is what a station broadcasting does.

entries.clue: Reeling, when getting religious in pub (2,1,4)

indicatorNotes.in: In puts one thing inside another, so the pieces named before it go between the letters of the word that comes after.

blocks.note: the village inn is the pub, and its three letters split two and one
as and when are the same little word of timing — as I arrived, when I arrived
pi is old school slang for pious, said of somebody ostentatiously religious

annotation.surface: Somebody staggering about after finding religion in a pub.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Religious' is two letters of schoolboy slang: pi, clipped from pious. The pub breaks open after two of its three letters, which puts the join in an unlikely place.
annotation.definitionFit: To be in a spin is to be reeling — head going round, unable to think straight.

entries.clue: Titled man protecting head beginning to enter foreign parliament (7)

indicatorNotes.protecting: Something protecting a thing stands around it, shielding it, so the word named first closes over what comes next.

blocks.note: Kt is the short form of Knight written after a name, and the two letters part to take the rest
a ness is a headland — Sheerness, Dungeness — the head of land that juts into the sea
the letter standing at the beginning of the word enter

annotation.surface: A knight shielding a head as it starts to go into a foreign assembly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Head' is the geographer's one, a ness, and the knight arrives as two letters rather than as a word. The Knesset is Israel's single chamber, a hundred and twenty members sitting in Jerusalem.
annotation.definitionFit: The Knesset is the parliament of Israel, so the definition points at it by nationality rather than by name.

entries.clue: Snatches Americans (5)

blocks.note: the verb: to yank a rope is to pull it sharply
the British nickname for them, in general use since the GIs came over

annotation.surface: Grabbing hold of some visiting Americans.
annotation.walkthrough: Two words of clue and no wordplay at all, so each word has to define the answer by itself. One sense takes a capital letter and the other does not, a difference the grid has no way of showing.
annotation.definitionFit: To yank something is to snatch it with a sharp pull; and Yanks is the British nickname for Americans, in general use since the GIs came over in the 1940s.

entries.clue: Climbing a great deal, late, pull up abruptly (4,4)

indicatorNotes.Climbing: Climbing goes up the page, so in a down entry the word named after it is read from its last letter back to its first.

blocks.note: pots of money is a great deal of it, and pots carries the quantity on its own
the late Mr So-and-so is the dead one

annotation.surface: A climber, high up and running behind, hauls himself to a halt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Late' is the obituary sense rather than the clock's, though the clock is what the climb offers first. Climbing only turns a word round in a down entry, where up the page runs backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: To stop dead is to halt on the instant with no slowing first, which is what pulling up abruptly describes.
